interview_metadata.name: Michael Barron
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Well, I'll do my best to keep it short, though my wife Susan would tell you I never do. I was born in 1958 in Gresham, Oregon, about ten miles east of Portland. My folks were Lloyd and Marjorie Barron — Dad worked at the Reynolds aluminum plant in Troutdale most of his life, and Mom kept the books at a small dental office in Gresham. We weren't wealthy but we never went hungry. I'm the middle of three; older sister Linda, younger brother Doug. We grew up in a little four-bedroom on the edge of town with a workshop my granddad had built in the 1920s — that's really where everything started for me. I spent every Saturday out there from about age eight on, watching him plane down cedar and oak, and by twelve I was building birdhouses to sell at the church bazaar. I went to Sam Barlow High, graduated in '76, then did two years of business courses at Mt. Hood Community College — I figured a tradesman ought to know how to read a balance sheet, and that's turned out to be true. I never finished the degree because I got an apprenticeship with a cabinetmaker named Hal Greer in southeast Portland, and I learned more in those four years under him than any classroom would've given me. I made master carpenter by the time I was thirty. I met Susan in 1982 at a church potluck in Fairview, and we married in 1984. We've got two children — our son Daniel, he's forty, lives in Hillsboro and does software work; and our daughter Rachel, thirty-seven, she's a nurse in Bend with two of our grandkids. Susan and I bought our place here in Fairview in 1988, and I ran my own small carpentry outfit, Barron Custom Woodwork, until I retired four years ago at sixty-three. Biggest life events? Losing my dad in 2007 to a heart attack hit hard. The 1996 flood took my workshop and most of my tools — that was a setback. And of course retirement itself, which I'm still adjusting to. That's the short version, anyway.

follow_ups.question: You said your granddad's workshop is where it all started. What's the first thing you remember building entirely on your own?
follow_ups.response: A little three-legged stool when I was about ten. Granddad let me pick the wood — I chose walnut because I liked how it smelled when you cut it. He stood over me but didn't touch a thing. Took me most of a Saturday and it wobbled, but I still have it out in the garage.

follow_ups.question: Tell me more about Hal Greer's shop. What was a typical day there like?
follow_ups.response: Six AM start, sharp. Hal didn't tolerate lateness. We'd sweep the shop first thing, then he'd hand out the day's work — a kitchen run, a built-in, whatever. He taught us to measure twice and then measure once more, and to always leave the shop cleaner than we found it. Lunch was sandwiches on the loading dock at noon, and we'd be out the door by four-thirty. He paid fair and he never raised his voice, but you knew when you'd disappointed him.

follow_ups.question: What was hardest about retiring at sixty-three?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, the silence. For forty-some years my day started with the radio in the shop and the smell of sawdust. The first month of retirement I'd wander out to the garage at seven AM and just stand there. Took me a good year to get a new rhythm — the historical society work and the volunteer mentoring helped more than I expected.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes, I'd say there was. The summer after my second year at Mt. Hood, in 1978, I had two paths laid out pretty clearly. My mom's brother, Uncle Frank, had a foot in the door at a savings and loan in Portland and he was pushing me to take an entry job there — wear a tie, work my way up, pension at sixty-five. And on the other side, Hal Greer had offered me an apprenticeship that paid about half as much and meant four more years before I'd be considered competent at anything. My folks were split. Dad thought the bank was steadier, Mom said I should follow what I actually liked. I went back and forth on it for about two weeks. What tipped me was a Saturday I spent in Hal's shop just sitting in on a job — I watched him fit a drawer slide and the satisfaction on his face when it ran clean, that was something I'd never seen on a banker's face. I called Uncle Frank the next Monday and told him no. He didn't speak to me at family dinners for about a year. But that decision set the whole shape of my life — the trade, the shop, eventually meeting Susan through one of Hal's other apprentices. So yes, that was the crossroads.

follow_ups.question: Did your uncle ever come around?
follow_ups.response: He did, eventually. About 1984, when I built him and Aunt Carol a dining table for their anniversary, he ran his hand across the top and said, 'Alright, Mike, alright.' That was about as much as I was going to get from him, and it was enough.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever wondered what life would've been like on the banker's path?
follow_ups.response: Now and then, especially when the bills were tight in the eighties. But no, not seriously. I think I'd have been miserable in a tie.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. I deliberated on it for weeks, talked it over with my folks, and made the call myself. Nothing just happened to me about that one.

follow_ups.question: Does that pattern hold for other big decisions in your life?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, yes. I'm a planner. Susan jokes I have a spreadsheet for everything, which isn't far off.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Hal himself was the helping hand, really. He didn't pressure me, he just laid out what the apprenticeship would be and let me decide. I don't think I needed anyone else. The carpenters' local was helpful later on for the paperwork side.

follow_ups.question: Would a younger person today have the same options you had?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, fewer. The trades have been hollowed out. That's part of why I mentor — to keep that ladder there for somebody.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: Susan is at the center of everything. We've been married forty-two years this June. She retired from elementary school teaching two years ago — she taught third grade at Fairview Elementary for nearly three decades — and we've been figuring out retirement together, which has its moments but mostly it's a gift. Our son Daniel is forty, lives in Hillsboro with his wife Beth, and they have a boy, Liam, who's nine. Daniel does software for a healthcare company; we don't share a vocabulary on what he actually does but he's good at it. Rachel, our daughter, is thirty-seven, a registered nurse at St. Charles in Bend. She married Tom about ten years ago and they have Eliza, eight, and Ben, five. We drive to Bend every six weeks or so — the kids are at the age where if you miss two months they've grown out of their shoes. My brother Doug is sixty-four, lives in Vancouver, Washington, and we see him on holidays. My sister Linda passed in 2019 from cancer; that was a hard one, she was seventy. Susan's parents are both gone now too — her mom in 2015, her dad in 2020. So the family's gotten smaller at the top and is growing at the bottom, which is the way it should be, I suppose.

follow_ups.question: What does a visit to Bend usually look like?
follow_ups.response: We leave Fairview Friday around two, get in by five-thirty if traffic on 26 cooperates. Rachel cooks Friday night, we take the grandkids to Drake Park Saturday morning, I usually fix something around their house — last trip it was a sticking storm door — and we drive back Sunday afternoon. Same rhythm most visits.

follow_ups.question: Tell me more about Liam — what's he into?
follow_ups.response: Lego, mostly, and he's started showing an interest in the workshop, which warms my heart. Last Christmas I had him sand a little box he'd helped me glue up. He's careful with his hands like his grandmother.

follow_ups.question: How did Linda's passing change family dynamics?
follow_ups.response: She was the one who held holidays together — every Thanksgiving was at her house in Beaverton. After she went, Susan and I took on hosting, but it's quieter now. We still set her place sometimes, by accident.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: Just Susan's sister Karen, in Salem. She and Susan talk on the phone every Sunday. I get along with her fine, but we're not close — she's a city person and we're not.

follow_ups.question: Any cousins or extended family in the area?
follow_ups.response: A few Barron cousins still around Gresham, but we mostly just exchange Christmas cards now.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yes, a handful. There's Ray Mendoza — he was one of Hal Greer's apprentices same time as me, and we've stayed close almost fifty years. He lives in Troutdale, we fish together on the Columbia most summer Saturdays. There's Pastor Dale Hutchins at our church, First Methodist in Fairview — he's about my age and we sit on the historical society board together. And there's Walt Pearson, who runs the walking club at the community center; I see him three mornings a week. Then there's a younger fellow, Marcus, twenty-six, who I've been mentoring through the carpenters' local for about two years now. He comes by the shop Saturdays.

follow_ups.question: How did the mentorship with Marcus start?
follow_ups.response: The local apprenticeship program asked if any retired masters would take on a mentee, and I said yes. Marcus had been bouncing between gigs and needed somebody to slow him down and teach him to think about a project before he started cutting. He's coming along.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Ray talk about out on the river?
follow_ups.response: Not much, honestly. That's the appeal. We compare flies, complain about our knees, and watch the water. Maybe an hour total of actual conversation across a whole day.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We're in the older part of Fairview, just east of 223rd, in a neighborhood that went up mostly in the late seventies. Our street is a quiet loop, maybe thirty houses, all single-family on quarter-acre lots. Big firs, mature gardens, a lot of folks who've been here as long as we have. Fairview itself is a small city, around eleven thousand people, between Gresham and Troutdale, easy reach of Portland but with a small-town feel. The Columbia is ten minutes north, the Sandy River about the same east. The community center is a five-minute drive, the church is walking distance, and there's a Fred Meyer and a couple grocery stores within ten minutes. We've got the gorge to the east — Multnomah Falls is a half-hour drive if there's no traffic. It's a comfortable place to live and we've never seriously considered moving.

follow_ups.question: How well do you know your immediate neighbors?
follow_ups.response: Real well. On either side it's the Petersens — Frank and Lorraine, they've been there since '91 — and the Wus, who moved in about 2018. Across the street is the Marsh family with two teenagers. We share tools and watch each other's mail when folks travel.

follow_ups.question: Has the neighborhood changed much over the decades?
follow_ups.response: Some. More renters now, a few short-term rentals which I'm not crazy about. The Marshes' house was a starter home for a young couple back in the eighties; now it would sell for more than I paid for ours three times over.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel safe, very safe. We don't lock the back door during the day. There was a car break-in down the block last summer, which got everybody's attention, but that's the exception. The fire station is a mile away and response times are good.

follow_ups.question: Does Susan feel as safe as you do?
follow_ups.response: She's a little more cautious — she locks the front door when I'm out in the shop. But she's not anxious about it.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Mostly ups. Good neighbors, mild weather, beautiful country in every direction. The downs would be the traffic on I-84 has gotten brutal, and property taxes keep climbing, which on a fixed income is something we pay attention to. But there's no place we'd rather be.

follow_ups.question: Have property taxes ever made you consider downsizing?
follow_ups.response: We've talked about it once or twice. Not seriously yet. The house is paid off, and moving costs would eat any savings.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: It's just Susan and me. Our dog Buster, a ten-year-old yellow lab, but I don't think he counts on the census. The kids have their own places. Sometimes the grandkids stay over for a long weekend, but that's it.

follow_ups.question: How often do the grandkids come stay?
follow_ups.response: Liam from Hillsboro maybe one weekend a month. The Bend grandkids come up around school breaks — usually a week at Christmas, a week in the summer.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone's permanent. Just Susan and me, and Buster.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Just the grandkids on visits, and my brother Doug on the occasional holiday.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody. It's just us.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: I'm a creature of routine, so the variation is small. Up at five-thirty every day, coffee, the Oregonian on my tablet, breakfast with Susan around six-thirty. Monday, Wednesday, Friday I do the walking club at the community center, seven to eight AM. Tuesday and Thursday I'm in the workshop most of the morning. Wednesdays I have a historical society meeting from one to three. Thursday afternoon I do the household bookkeeping — pay bills, reconcile accounts, that kind of thing. Saturday mornings, summer especially, Ray and I fish. Saturday afternoons Marcus comes by the shop. Sunday it's church at nine-thirty, lunch out with Susan after, and a quiet afternoon. Cabin renovation I work on as weather allows.

follow_ups.question: What time do you typically go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Nine-thirty most nights. Ten on a Saturday if there's a Trail Blazers game.

follow_ups.question: Does Susan keep a similar schedule?
follow_ups.response: Close to it. She sleeps in a little later — six-thirty — and she has a book club Tuesday evenings I'm not part of.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I'm retired from paid work. I closed Barron Custom Woodwork in 2022. Now my time goes to three unpaid things: the historical society books, the carpenters' apprentice mentoring, and our property renovation. The historical society work I do Wednesday afternoons mostly, sometimes a few hours at home reconciling. Mentoring is Saturday afternoons. The cabin renovation — we have a small cabin on the back of our property I'm restoring — that's whenever the weather allows, usually weekdays.

follow_ups.question: Do you miss the paid work?
follow_ups.response: Bits of it. I miss the satisfaction of a finished kitchen, and the customer's face. I don't miss the bidding, the chasing payments, or the paperwork.

follow_ups.question: How many hours a week would you say the volunteer work adds up to?
follow_ups.response: Maybe fifteen, twenty. Some weeks more, some less.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I tend the vegetable garden — that's spring through fall, almost daily. Tomatoes, beans, zucchini, some lettuce, herbs. I do all the yard work and the home maintenance — Susan won't go near a ladder anymore. I keep up our two vehicles, oil changes and the like. And I'm the official walker of Buster, morning and evening.

follow_ups.question: What's the biggest thing in your garden right now?
follow_ups.response: The tomatoes are still seedlings — we get them in around Mother's Day. But the rhubarb is going crazy, and we'll have lettuce in another two weeks.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Susan's retirement two years ago was the biggest change. We had to learn how to share the house all day, which sounds simple but it isn't after forty years of each going off to work. We worked out little rules — she has the kitchen mornings, I have it afternoons; we have lunch together; we each have one solo evening a week. Beyond that, I started the walking club last fall on doctor's recommendation, and the mentoring with Marcus is about two years in.

follow_ups.question: What prompted the walking club?
follow_ups.response: My GP wanted my blood pressure down, and I'd been more sedentary than I should be in retirement. The community center group is free and there's accountability — if I don't show up, Walt calls me.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are grown, so this would apply to the grandkids really. Liam, in Hillsboro, is in third grade — Daniel and Beth drop him at school by eight, after-school he's in a Lego club Wednesdays and soccer on Thursdays. Eliza in Bend is in second grade, does ballet Tuesdays. Ben is in pre-K, hasn't picked up activities yet beyond chasing the dog.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever do school pickup for Liam?
follow_ups.response: When Daniel needs us, yes. Susan and I will drive over to Hillsboro for a Wednesday and get Liam from Lego club, take him to dinner. We did that maybe four times last fall.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Very few. A speeding ticket on I-84 back in the nineties, that's the worst of it. I went to a citizens' police academy thing the Fairview police ran about ten years ago, which was interesting. I know two of the patrol officers by name from church. Nothing dramatic.

follow_ups.question: What was the citizens' academy like?
follow_ups.response: Eight weeks, Tuesday evenings. They walked us through how they do traffic stops, use of force, the dispatch center. I came away with more respect for the job and more questions about training.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: The 1996 flood — sheriff's deputies came door-to-door to check on people. That was a good interaction. Otherwise nothing memorable.

follow_ups.question: Did the deputies help with anything specific?
follow_ups.response: They helped me move tools out of the workshop before the water got higher. I won't forget that.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: None in my immediate family. A high-school friend got picked up for a DUI back in the eighties; that's the closest I've been to it.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in every election, including the local ones — school board, water district, the lot. Oregon is vote-by-mail, so it's easy. Susan and I sit at the kitchen table with the voters' pamphlet a week before ballots are due and go through every measure together. We've done that since we moved here in '88.

follow_ups.question: Have you and Susan always agreed on candidates?
follow_ups.response: Not always. We've canceled each other out on a presidential or two. We don't make a fuss about it.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'd call myself moderate-conservative. Fiscally conservative, mostly — I believe in living within your means whether you're a household or a government. I'm skeptical of big new programs unless someone can show me how they pay for themselves. Socially, I'm more moderate than the national Republican Party has gone — I think marriage is between whoever wants to commit, I don't have a problem with that. I'm a strong supporter of the trades and apprenticeship programs, and I think we've under-invested in vocational education for forty years. On guns, I own a couple — a deer rifle and an old shotgun — and I believe in responsible ownership and reasonable background checks; I don't see those as conflicting. On the environment, I'm more conservation-minded than most of my party — you can't grow up in the Columbia Gorge and not care about it. I'm pro-veteran, pro-small-business. Where I part with the modern Democratic side is mostly on spending and on what I see as a lack of seriousness about the border. Where I part with the modern Republican side is on tone, on conspiracies, and on character — I have no patience for any of it.

follow_ups.question: Has the Republican Party changed in ways that bother you?
follow_ups.response: Considerably, since about 2016. I voted Republican most of my life, but I've split my ticket more in the last decade than I ever did before. Reagan I'd have walked through fire for; today's brand is a different animal.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with friends?
follow_ups.response: Carefully. Ray is more conservative than I am, Pastor Dale's more moderate, Walt at the walking club leans liberal. We've got a rule: no politics before nine AM. We mostly stick to it.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: The biggest change is I've become more independent. I used to register Republican and vote the straight ticket; now I'm registered as a non-affiliated voter and I split my ballot regularly. I'd say the move started around 2016, accelerated through the pandemic, and feels settled now. I've also gotten more skeptical of party media on both sides — I used to listen to talk radio in the shop and I've cut most of it out. I read the Oregonian and the Wall Street Journal opinion pages and try to make up my own mind.

follow_ups.question: What pushed you away from talk radio?
follow_ups.response: The temperature got too high. I noticed I was angrier after I listened, and I wasn't learning anything. I'd rather listen to Neko Case or an audiobook on Oregon history.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat. I'm a white man in a mostly white town, so it's not at my doorstep. But Portland was at the center of the 2020 protests and Fairview is fifteen miles east of that, so it was on the news every night and we couldn't help but take it in. I had hard conversations with my daughter Rachel — she's more progressive than I am and she pushed me to read some things I wouldn't have picked up otherwise. I'd say I came out of that period with more sympathy for the basic concern than I went in with, and also more skepticism about some of the specific policy proposals.

follow_ups.question: What did Rachel have you read?
follow_ups.response: A book called The Warmth of Other Suns, by Isabel Wilkerson. That was a serious piece of history and I was glad I read it. We didn't agree on everything afterward, but I understood her better.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the basic concern — that Black Americans have had a different experience with police and with the courts — is real and documented. I don't think 'defund the police' is the right answer, and that slogan probably set back the legitimate reforms. I think we need better-trained officers, better mental health response, and accountability when things go wrong. I also think it's a longer conversation than any of us are going to settle in this room.

follow_ups.question: Has your view changed over the last five years?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I take the concerns more seriously than I did. I also have less patience for some of the louder voices on both sides.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: It's the country's oldest unresolved problem and I don't expect it to go away in my lifetime. I think the progress is real and so is the work that's left. I worry that people are talking past each other more than they're listening. Locally, Multnomah County has gotten more diverse since we moved here and I think that's been good for the place overall.

follow_ups.question: Have you noticed changes in Fairview specifically?
follow_ups.response: Some, yes. The school is more diverse than it was in the eighties when our kids went through. The church has a small but growing Korean fellowship that meets in the basement Sunday afternoons.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I've talked with family — mostly Rachel and Susan — and a little with friends. I haven't joined a protest. Not really my style; I'm more of a one-on-one conversation person.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Mixed. Rachel was very engaged, went to a couple of protests in Bend in 2020. Daniel's quieter about it, I don't fully know where he lands. Ray's more skeptical of the whole movement than I am. Pastor Dale led a small adult-ed class at the church on it that was thoughtful. So a wide range, even in my small circle.

follow_ups.question: Did Pastor Dale's class shift anyone's views that you noticed?
follow_ups.response: It softened a few. The format was good — small groups, one chapter at a time, no shouting. That's how minds change, when they do.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: I'm sixty-seven and overall in good shape, but not without issues. I have moderately high blood pressure I manage with lisinopril, ten milligrams. I have arthritis in my hands and lower back — forty years of carpentry will do that. I had a knee scope in 2018 for a torn meniscus that's been fine since. Cholesterol is borderline; I'm on a low dose of atorvastatin. I see Dr. Holcomb at Adventist Medical Group twice a year. Sleep's pretty good — usually seven hours. Vision needs readers now.

follow_ups.question: How's the back arthritis on the worst days?
follow_ups.response: Stiff in the mornings, sometimes I can't bend to tie my shoes for the first hour. Heat and walking help. I take Advil maybe twice a week.

follow_ups.question: Any concerns coming up at your next checkup?
follow_ups.response: Dr. Holcomb wants to talk about my A1C — it's been creeping. So we'll see.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy: routine. I eat about the same things, walk regularly, sleep regular hours. Susan cooks well and we don't keep junk in the house. Hard: the desk side of retirement — I sit more than I used to. And I have a sweet tooth — apple crumble is my weakness.

follow_ups.question: How often do you indulge the sweet tooth?
follow_ups.response: Sunday dessert after church lunch, usually. Once a week, I keep it to that.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Two things. About fourteen months ago, in early 2025, I had a bad arthritis flare in my right hand that put me out of the workshop for nearly two months. Cortisone shot eventually settled it. And six months ago I had a sigmoidoscopy that found a couple of polyps; they were benign but they want me back in three years. Otherwise nothing major.

follow_ups.question: How did you handle the two months out of the shop?
follow_ups.response: Poorly at first. I got grumpy. Susan finally pointed out I could still read and still do the historical society books, so I leaned into that. The mentoring sessions with Marcus shifted to him doing the cutting and me supervising.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: The hand flare last year was the closest example. If I'd still been running the business I would have had to cancel jobs. In retirement it just meant a slower pace and disappointed myself. No childcare implications at my age.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes. Susan had a breast cancer scare in 2021 — a biopsy that came back benign, but the three weeks of waiting were the worst of my life. And my sister Linda's cancer, in 2018 and 2019, was hard. We drove to Beaverton a lot in those months. My mother is ninety-two and in an assisted living facility in Gresham, with dementia that's progressing; that's a slow grief.

follow_ups.question: How often do you visit your mother?
follow_ups.response: Every Tuesday afternoon, like clockwork. She doesn't always know me anymore, but she knows the voice.

follow_ups.question: How has Susan recovered from the scare?
follow_ups.response: Physically, fully. Psychologically, she's more vigilant about screenings, which I think is wise.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We've been fortunate. I'm on Medicare with a supplemental plan, Susan is on her teacher's retirement plan plus Medicare. Access has been pretty good — wait times for specialists can be six weeks, which is annoying but workable. No, I haven't forgone care. There were a couple of years in the nineties as a self-employed tradesman when I went without insurance and I kept my fingers crossed. We're past that.

follow_ups.question: Anything you'd change about the system?
follow_ups.response: Make it less complicated. The amount of paperwork around an MRI is absurd. But that's an old man complaining.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Not really. Susan got acupuncture for migraines a few years ago and felt it helped. I'm skeptical but not closed-minded. I'll take willow-bark tea for a headache before an aspirin sometimes, which my grandmother taught me.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I don't smoke. Never have, beyond a few teenage cigarettes I regret. I drink moderately — a beer with dinner most nights, a glass of red wine on Sundays, the occasional bourbon when Ray comes over. Never used it to cope; that's not the family I came from.

follow_ups.question: What kind of beer?
follow_ups.response: Whatever's on sale at Fred Meyer that isn't too hoppy. I like a brown ale or an amber.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: Just over-the-counter ibuprofen for the back and hands. I take it maybe twice a week. I haven't tried marijuana — it's legal here but I haven't gone there. I've used prescription pain medication exactly twice in my life, after the knee scope and after a wisdom tooth extraction. Both times for three days, then I stopped.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Medicare plus a Plan G supplemental for me, and Susan has PERS retiree health plus Medicare. Out-of-pocket runs us maybe four hundred a month between premiums and copays. We budget for it like any other line item. The bigger worry is long-term care if either of us ends up like my mother — that's a different math problem and we have a long-term care policy through AARP for some of it.

follow_ups.question: Have you looked into supplemental long-term care planning?
follow_ups.response: We met with a financial planner in 2023 and went through it. The policy we have covers about three years of skilled care for either of us. We're hoping we don't need it.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I'm pro-vaccination. I got my COVID shots, I get the flu shot every fall, I got the shingles vaccine, and Dr. Holcomb just talked me into the new RSV one. Always have, always will.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: Dr. Holcomb first. CDC website second. I'll read the Oregonian's health coverage. I do not trust Facebook for medical anything.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Overall, settled. Retirement is starting to feel like its own thing rather than a void. The hand flare in early 2025 was a low point — physically and mentally. There's a low-grade worry I carry about the future — money lasting, health holding, the country generally — but it's background noise, not foreground. Day to day I'm content. Susan and I are in a good rhythm. The grandkids are a joy. My mother's decline is the heaviest thing I'm carrying right now.

follow_ups.question: What does the background worry sound like, if you put words to it?
follow_ups.response: Will the savings last if one of us needs nursing care? Will the country still be a place where my grandkids can earn a living with their hands if they want to? Will I be the husband Susan needs if my health goes first? Those kinds of questions, at three AM sometimes.

follow_ups.question: What helps quiet those?
follow_ups.response: A morning walk. A finished piece in the shop. A good conversation with Pastor Dale. Sleep, frankly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last August, my mother had a fall and was hospitalized for a week. I drove to Gresham every day. She didn't recognize me by Wednesday. I came home Thursday night and sat in the workshop with the lights off for about an hour, just trying to absorb it. Susan found me out there. I told her I felt like I was losing my mother in slow motion and there was nothing useful I could do. That was the closest I've come to crying in a long while.

follow_ups.question: How did Susan respond?
follow_ups.response: She didn't try to fix it. She just sat with me. That was the right thing.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I wouldn't say I've ever been clinically depressed. I have a tendency toward worry — anxiety, mild, more about the future than the present. I went through a low patch in the year after Dad died, in 2007 and 2008. Pastor Dale at the time pointed me toward a counselor for a few sessions and that helped me put the loss in better order. Nothing since that's risen to that level.

follow_ups.question: Was therapy something you'd been open to before that?
follow_ups.response: Frankly, no. Men of my generation and background don't generally go. But Pastor Dale made it feel practical, not soft, and I came out of it better.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: Rachel had postpartum anxiety after Ben, in 2021. She got help quickly. Daniel has always been the steady one. Susan's had her hard moments but she's resilient.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Religion is important to me, though more quietly than loudly. I'm a Methodist, raised that way and stayed that way. Susan and I attend First United Methodist Church of Fairview, the nine-thirty service most Sundays. Pastor Dale Hutchins has been there about fifteen years and his preaching is thoughtful — not flashy, which suits me. I serve on the historical society board through the church and we've helped restore some old sanctuary records. My faith is more practical than mystical — I believe in showing up, doing the work, treating people right, and trusting that the rest is in better hands than mine. I pray, more in the morning than at night, usually short. I don't think God micromanages parking spaces. I do think a life is meant for something more than itself, and that keeps me oriented.

follow_ups.question: Has your faith changed over the years?
follow_ups.response: It's gotten quieter and more durable. Less certain about specifics, more certain about basics. I used to argue theology more; now I'd rather feed somebody.

follow_ups.question: Do the kids practice?
follow_ups.response: Daniel and Beth attend a church in Hillsboro, more contemporary than ours. Rachel went away from it in her twenties and is finding her way back now in Bend, last I heard at a small Episcopal parish.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I have Facebook, mainly to see grandkid photos and the church's announcements. I check it maybe three times a week, ten minutes at a stretch. I never post. I have no other social media — no Instagram, no Twitter or whatever it's called now, no TikTok. Susan is the same. I do use YouTube to watch woodworking videos and old film clips, but I don't have an account I post to. Email I use daily.

follow_ups.question: Anyone on Facebook you'd lose touch with if you weren't on it?
follow_ups.response: Probably a dozen old apprentices from over the years, and Susan's cousins back east. Yeah, I'd miss those threads.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: No. I'd talk to Susan or Pastor Dale before I'd post on Facebook about something hard. That's not a generation thing, that's just me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress is lower than during work years, but the worry about future health and finances has gone up a little. The walking club has been a quiet help. So has the mentoring — being useful to Marcus is a coping tool I didn't anticipate.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: Susan, my wife. And Buster, our dog. That's it.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: Susan and I share everything. House is paid off.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: Property tax installment was the biggest line, about $1,100. Then groceries around $650, utilities around $280, health insurance premiums about $400, gasoline around $180, the cabin project materials about $300. Plus the usual subscriptions and small stuff.

follow_ups.question: How do you track all that?
follow_ups.response: Spreadsheet. I update it Thursday afternoons. Habit from running the business.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: Last month we spent about $4,800. Usual is closer to $3,800. Property tax pushed it up. Most months we run between $3,500 and $4,200.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: We own. Paid the mortgage off in 2014. Best birthday present I've given myself.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Heating bill spikes January and February — runs $250 versus a summer $90. Property taxes hit in November and May, bigger than any single month otherwise. Christmas adds about $1,200 between gifts and travel to Bend. Garden inputs are higher in April. Cabin materials I batch in dry months. Otherwise it's pretty even.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: We have an emergency fund — about eight months of expenses — and a separate sinking fund for property tax and holidays. So most of what looks like a 'big' month is actually planned for.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: We save. We have a high-yield savings account at a credit union, a Roth IRA each, and traditional IRAs from rollovers from our working years. We also have a brokerage account with index funds I don't touch much. We try to add to the savings account monthly even now, though the amount is smaller in retirement.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: Rainy day mostly. And for travel — we're putting away for an England trip in 2027, my long-held dream to visit Bath. Some for grandkids' education, modest amounts.

follow_ups.question: What draws you to Bath?
follow_ups.response: Maritime and architectural history, mostly, and the Barron name traces vaguely back to Somerset. I want to see the Roman baths and the Royal Crescent before my knees give out.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: None. We pay credit cards in full every month. The house is paid off. We bought our truck used in cash. No loans of any kind.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: Hasn't happened in the past year. Honestly, hasn't happened since the late nineties when business was thin. We've been disciplined.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Master carpenter, retired. I ran a small custom woodworking business, Barron Custom Woodwork, from 1990 to 2022. Specialty was custom kitchens, built-in cabinetry, and the occasional piece of furniture. Duties were everything from the initial customer meeting and rough sketch, to materials sourcing, milling, joinery, finishing, installation, and follow-up service. I did most of the work myself with one apprentice at a time. Bookkeeping, taxes, insurance, scheduling — all me, with Susan's help on the books some years.

follow_ups.question: Favorite piece you ever built?
follow_ups.response: A walnut sideboard for a family in Lake Oswego in 2009. Hand-cut dovetails, hidden compartments, finished with oil and wax. They sent a Christmas card every year after.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: I was a member of the Pacific Northwest Regional Council of Carpenters during my apprentice and journeyman years. When I went out on my own I dropped active membership, but I've stayed connected through the apprenticeship program, which is how I came to mentor Marcus.

transcript.question_text: In the past year, how many weeks did you work (for a few hours, including paid vacation, paid sick leave, and military service)?
transcript.response: Zero paid weeks. I'm retired.

transcript.question_text: How many hours each week did you usually work?
transcript.response: Zero paid hours. Maybe twenty unpaid hours volunteering and on the cabin.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: No paid work at all.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Zero.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: From employment, nothing. I receive Social Security — about $2,400 a month — and IRA withdrawals we manage to a budget.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: Social Security comes monthly. IRA distributions I take quarterly.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: Roughly $6,800 combined — my Social Security, Susan's PERS pension and Social Security, and the planned IRA draw.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yes. Always. I do them with TurboTax, married filing jointly. We sent it off in early April.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job? (This could include things like health benefits, paid time off, vacation, and sick time.)
transcript.response: Not applicable — retired. When I ran the business I had no employer benefits; we bought our own insurance.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: I was the boss. Relationships with apprentices were teacher-student, mostly good. Customers were generally repeat or referral.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: When I was working I set my own hours but I was disciplined — six AM to four-thirty PM most days, half-day Saturdays when a job demanded. Flexibility was high in theory; in practice I kept it tight.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Susan stayed teaching through the kids' school years and we coordinated around school schedules. It was tight but manageable.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No. Just Social Security retirement and Medicare.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: Income is flat in retirement — Social Security and pension don't vary. No especially low months this year.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: I'd write a check from the emergency fund and not feel it. That's what the fund is for.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Comfortable, with reservations. We're not wealthy, but we have no debt, the house is ours, we have savings and reasonable retirement income. The reservation is long-term care — that's the wild card. And inflation on fixed-ish income makes me watch the spreadsheet. But on the whole, we did what we said we'd do and it's working.

follow_ups.question: What's the one financial decision you're proudest of?
follow_ups.response: Paying off the house early. We doubled mortgage payments through the 2000s and got it done in 2014. The peace of mind from that is worth more than the math.

transcript.question_text: Are you now married, widowed, divorced, separated, or have you never been married? If you are not currently married, are you currently living with a romantic partner?
transcript.response: Married. To Susan. Since June 16, 1984.

transcript.question_text: For our records, we also need your date of birth. Could you please provide that?
Were you born in the United States? If you were not born in the U.S., what country were you born, and what year did you first come to the U.S. to live?
transcript.response: Yes, born in the U.S. — Gresham, Oregon.

transcript.question_text: What city and state were you born in?
transcript.response: Gresham, Oregon.

transcript.question_text: Are you of Hispanic, Latinx, or Spanish origin?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: What race or races do you identify with?
transcript.response: White. English and Scots-Irish background as far as I know.

transcript.question_text: What is the highest degree or grade you've completed?
transcript.response: Some college — two years at Mt. Hood Community College, no degree. Plus my carpenters' apprenticeship completion, which functioned like a degree in my field.

transcript.question_text: Are you enrolled in school?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Have you been enrolled in school during the past 3 months?
transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Have you ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard?
transcript.response: No. My number didn't come up in the late draft years; I was finishing high school in '76 when the draft was inactive.

transcript.question_text: What religion do you identify with, if any?
transcript.response: United Methodist — Protestant Christian.

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: Officially non-affiliated. Functionally an independent who leans Republican on fiscal issues and is more mixed on social ones. I've voted both ways in the last decade. I don't strongly associate with either party right now.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?
transcript.response: Slightly closer to the Republican Party, historically. Less so today than ten years ago.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Gresham, Oregon.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: Yes, both. Lloyd and Marjorie. Together their whole marriage until Dad died in 2007.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: My sister Linda, who was eighteen and about to leave for school, and my brother Doug, who was thirteen.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: High school diploma. He took some night classes in welding later on.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: Two-year secretarial certificate from a business school in Portland.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, the whole time. Part-time when we were small, full-time once we were in school.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Office manager and bookkeeper for a small dental practice in Gresham — Dr. Halverson's. She ran the front desk, did the books, managed billing and insurance. She was the operation behind the operation.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: A small dental office — one dentist, one hygienist, one assistant, and Mom. General dentistry. She was there twenty-four years.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, the whole time. Steady employment.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Industrial maintenance and welder at the Reynolds Metals aluminum plant in Troutdale. He kept the production equipment running — maintenance, repairs, custom fabrication. Shift work, union member with the United Steelworkers.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: Reynolds Metals, large aluminum smelting and reduction plant. They produced aluminum ingots and rolled aluminum for industrial use. Big operation — a thousand-plus workers at its peak. The plant closed in 2000, but he'd retired in '98.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: I hope to keep most of what I have. Susan healthy and at my side. The kids and grandkids close enough to see often. Buster, or some dog after him. The shop still functioning, the garden still producing. What I'd add: the Bath trip in 2027 — I want to make that happen while I can still manage stairs. I'd like the cabin renovation finished, maybe within two years. I'd like Marcus to be running his own shop by the time he's thirty. I'd like to leave the historical society's books in better order than I found them. And I'd like, when my time comes, for it to come at home, not in a facility. That last part is more in God's hands than mine.

follow_ups.question: What's the next step on the Bath trip?
follow_ups.response: Susan's pricing flights for next spring. We're aiming at a two-week swing through Bath, the Cotswolds, and maybe up to York.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Family first. Susan, the kids, the grandkids. After that, the work I've done with my hands — what's outlasted me already in those kitchens and pieces around the region. After that, this community — the church, the historical society, the apprentices. And quiet — the value of a peaceful, well-ordered life. That's what I've spent fifty years building, and I don't want anything else.

summaries.demographer: Michael Barron is a 67-year-old white, non-Hispanic, U.S.-born married male of English/Scots-Irish ancestry, residing in the older single-family section of Fairview, OR (97024), with deep multi-generational regional roots and an English-only, Protestant (United Methodist) cultural frame (Q85–Q97). He is retired, with 'some college' attainment (two years at Mt. Hood Community College plus a completed carpenters' apprenticeship), reflecting a working-class mobility pathway typical of mid-century Pacific Northwest trades (Q1, Q90). His household is a stable two-person retired couple — wife Susan, retired teacher — in a fully paid-off home owned since 1988, with three grandchildren divided between Hillsboro and Bend (Q5, Q58, Q83). Life-course markers include a 1984 marriage, 1990 self-employment launch, 2014 mortgage payoff, and 2022 retirement, placing him in a financially secure, late-life consolidation stage with high institutional embeddedness (church, historical society, trades) and no household dependents (Q11, Q15, Q83).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Michael's choice architecture is characterized by routine, deliberate budgeting, and strong loss aversion under a generally conservative time preference; he saves with sinking funds for predictable shocks (property tax, holidays) and an 8-month emergency fund, carries zero debt, and pays credit cards in full monthly (Q56, Q60, Q63, Q83). His career-defining crossroads — turning down a guaranteed banker's path for a longer, lower-paid apprenticeship — was an explicit, deliberated trade of short-term security for long-term identity payoff, signaling intrinsic-motivation orientation and identity-based decision making (Q2, Q3). He responds to incentives via routinization (Thursday spreadsheet, weekly mentor meetings, daily morning walks) rather than novelty; peer influence is high within his small trust network (Hal Greer, Ray Mendoza, Pastor Dale, GP Holcomb) and low from broader social media, which he deliberately under-uses (Q15, Q42, Q48). Anticipated long-term-care costs are his salient risk concern, addressed via a multi-year LTC policy purchased after a 2023 financial-planner consultation — a textbook ambiguity-aversion response (Q40).
summaries.political_scientist: Michael presents as a high-information, high-participation civic actor: votes in every election including local races, deliberates over the voter pamphlet with his spouse, and has personal acquaintance with local officers and clergy, all consistent with strong place-based institutional trust and community attachment (Q20, Q23, Q47). His partisan trajectory shows clear de-alignment: a lifelong Republican-leaning voter who re-registered as non-affiliated and now splits tickets, attributing the shift to perceived character and tone problems in the post-2016 GOP while retaining fiscal-conservative and traditional-values priors (Q24, Q25, Q95, Q96). On race and policing he occupies a deliberative center — sympathetic to BLM's underlying concerns and willing to engage in cross-perspective reading and family dialogue, while skeptical of 'defund' framing — indicating moderate openness to attitude updating in low-pressure deliberative settings (Q26–Q30). Institutional trust is high for local government, churches, his GP, the CDC, and legacy print media; low for talk radio and social-media-mediated information (Q42, Q25, Q48).
summaries.psychologist: Michael's personality profile reads as high conscientiousness and moderate-to-low extraversion with elevated dispositional worry (mild trait anxiety) but high emotional regulation supported by routine, manual work, and small-network confiding (Q15, Q43, Q45). His self-concept is craft-anchored — 'a tradesman ought to know how to read a balance sheet' — and reinforced through productive activities (workshop, garden, mentoring) that he uses instrumentally to convert distress into agency, evidenced during the 2025 hand flare and his mother's August 2025 hospitalization (Q1, Q33, Q44, Q50). Coping style is approach-oriented (talking with Susan or Pastor Dale, brief CBT-style counseling after his father's death) rather than avoidant or substance-mediated; substance use is non-functional and ritualized (Q38, Q39, Q45). Motivationally he is driven by generativity (mentoring Marcus, leaving organized affairs and historical-society books in better order than he found them) and legacy continuity, aligning with classic late-adulthood Eriksonian themes and explicit longing for a 'peaceful, well-ordered life' he can hand down (Q108, Q109).
